prompt: Match each failure to the cheapest level of test that would have caught it.
left: A currency helper rounds 0.125 down when the rule says round up
One module writes a date as a string and the module that reads it expects a number
Login still works, but after a route rename the button that starts a session does nothing
right: an integration test that runs the two modules together
an end-to-end test driving the real interface
a unit test on a single function

prompt: A suite is 200 browser-driven tests, and each one independently fails about 1% of the time for reasons unrelated to any real bug. Roughly what share of runs come back fully green?
options: About 99%
About 87%
About 13%
About 1%

prompt: A teammate wants to delete every unit test, arguing that only the end-to-end suite proves a user can complete a task. Make the case for keeping them without claiming the end-to-end tests are worthless.
criteria: Names the feedback loop: a unit test fails in seconds, a full end-to-end run takes minutes
Says an end-to-end failure tells you something broke but not which line broke it
Concedes that only the top level exercises the real wiring between parts
Argues for keeping both levels with most of the count sitting at the fastest one

prompt: A team keeps its 40 slow interface tests exactly as they are but goes from shipping once a week to shipping eight times a day. What gives way first, and what do people start doing about it?
criteria: Says total run time becomes the bottleneck on every single release
Predicts that intermittent failures get re-run rather than investigated
Names the moment a red suite stops being treated as a reason to stop
Proposes moving coverage down to faster levels instead of deleting tests

prompt: Put the steps of turning a reported bug into a permanent test into the order you would actually do them.
items: Change the code until the new test passes
Reproduce the bug by hand and pin down the exact input that triggers it
Write a test asserting the behaviour you wanted, and watch it fail
Leave the test in the suite so the same bug cannot come back unnoticed

prompt: This test was added to lock in a fix for a bug where paying twice charged the card twice. Which line means it would have passed before the fix as well?
why: `>= 1` is satisfied whether the second charge was suppressed or not, so the buggy code passes this test too. The assertion has to be `== 1` for the test to have anything to do with the bug.

prompt: Why is a test written after a fix, and green on its very first run, weaker evidence than one that was seen to fail?
criteria: States that a test green on the first run may never touch the buggy path
Says the red-then-green transition is what proves the test is wired to the bug
Notes that such a test can stay green even if the fix is later reverted
Says running it against the unfixed code is how you check it is real

prompt: A ticket says a report double-counted rows for one account. The engineer fixes the join, then adds a test that loads the full fixture and asserts the report total equals 41,208. Critique that test as protection against the bug returning.
criteria: Says the bare total gives no hint which behaviour is under test
Notes the assertion will fail on any unrelated change to the fixture
Says it never isolates the duplicated rows that caused the bug
Proposes a minimal case: one account with the key that duplicated

prompt: You have one hour to add tests to a module. Which of these are worth spending it on?
options: A function that turns a score ratio into a grade across four thresholds
A getter that returns a stored name unchanged
The branch that decides whether a due item or a brand-new item fills a slot
A wrapper that calls one library function and returns its result untouched
The date arithmetic that turns an interval in days into a next-due date

prompt: Fill in the blanks: tests earn their keep on ______ logic — the `if` and the `else` — and on ______ values, where a comparison such as `>=` flips from one result to the other.
Coverage on a module reads 94% and someone asks you to spend the afternoon on the last 6%. Describe when that is the wrong use of the afternoon, and what you would write instead.
criteria: Names pass-through or generated lines as uncovered code not worth a test
States that coverage counts lines executed, not assertions made
Gives an already-covered branch or boundary as the better target
Says a line can be covered by a test that asserts nothing about it

prompt: A scheduling function takes a grade from 0 to 5 plus the current interval, and takes a different path on a failing grade. Estimate how many test cases it takes to pin its behaviour down, and say what each one is for.
criteria: Lands on a count somewhere around 6 to 12 rather than one per input value
Includes a case on each side of the pass/fail grade boundary
Names a first-review case where the interval starts from zero
Treats the failing path as needing its own case, not a variant of the passing one
Says adding cases that only re-check the same branch does not raise the count

prompt: A save-it-for-later box asks for the text, a topic, a source link and a priority before the save button turns on. What is the most likely state of things six weeks later?
options: A tidy archive, because the metadata got filled in while the context was fresh
The same number of saves as a one-field box, since four fields take only a few seconds
Almost nothing saved, with the few entries arriving in bursts when someone feels dutiful
Plenty of saves, but with the priority field always left on its default

prompt: True or false: requiring one tag on every capture is a cheap addition, because typing a single word takes about three seconds.
criteria: Says the real cost is deciding which tag, not typing the word
States that a required field turns a reflex into a small task
Notes the cost is paid again on every capture, not once
Says the tag can be added later, when the item is actually reviewed

prompt: A product owner asks you to add three required fields to the capture screen so the data is clean from day one. Write the reply you would send.
criteria: Names the tradeoff between fields required and captures that happen at all
States the owner's real concern: usable data rather than a pile of loose text
Offers to infer or backfill the fields after the save instead of before
Lands on one recommendation rather than handing back a list of options

prompt: A screen for jotting things down opens with the cursor in a title field, has a category dropdown defaulting to Uncategorised, and saves from a button below the fold. Critique it for someone who wants to stash a paragraph in two seconds.
criteria: Says the cursor should start in the body field, not the title
Names the scroll or pointer trip to the save button as a cost paid every time
Says a keyboard save such as Ctrl+Enter removes that trip
Argues the title and category can be filled in silently and edited later

prompt: A bar chart compares 51% against 53%, and its vertical axis runs from 50% to 54%. How many times taller is the second bar as drawn?
explain: Bar height is measured from the axis floor, so the bars are 1 point and 3 points tall: the second is three times the first. A two-point gap on a scale that starts at zero would have looked like a 4% difference in height.

prompt: A line chart tracks a response time that sits between 240 ms and 260 ms all quarter. What does forcing its vertical axis to start at zero do?
options: Removes distortion, since a zero baseline is what makes any chart honest
Flattens the line into a near-straight band and hides the variation that matters
Nothing, because the shape of a line does not depend on the scale
Doubles the apparent size of every change

prompt: A colleague says "always start the axis at zero" is the only rule needed for honest charts. What does that rule get right, and where does it fall down?
criteria: States that a bar encodes its value as length, so it needs the zero baseline
Says a line carries change through slope rather than through length
Gives a case where a zero baseline hides variation that is the whole point
Names labelling the axis range as what keeps a truncated scale honest

prompt: A stakeholder asks you to crop the vertical axis on a bar chart so a 2% lift "reads as the win it is" in tomorrow's deck. Give your response.
criteria: Names that cropping the axis multiplies the apparent size of the difference
States the risk: the whole slide is doubted the moment someone reads the axis
Offers an alternative such as charting the change itself with the scale labelled
Does not stop at refusing — gives a way to make the 2% land as a win

prompt: A screen carries 22 tiles, everyone calls it useful, and nobody can say what it is for. What is the first move?
options: Move the least-viewed tiles onto a second tab
Ask what decision the screen is meant to support, then cut to the tiles that answer it
Add a filter bar so each team sees only the tiles it cares about
Sort the tiles by how often each one is looked at

prompt: Arrange these four elements from the top of a single-question screen down to what sits behind a click.
items: One number answering the question, next to its comparison with last period
A breakdown of that number by the two or three dimensions people ask about next
The question the screen answers, written out as the title

prompt: When is a dense grid of twenty small charts on one screen the right design rather than the wrong one?
criteria: Names live monitoring for anomalies as the case where scanning beats reading
States that the viewer already knows the normal shape of each panel
Says no single decision hangs on any one of the panels
Contrasts it with a screen built to answer one question for a reader

prompt: Four teams each want their two favourite charts on the one screen the leadership group looks at. Write what you say to all four of them.
criteria: Names the tradeoff: each tile added lowers the odds any tile gets read
States each team's real concern, which is their metric being ignored
Proposes a per-team screen plus one shared headline screen
Closes on a recommendation instead of a menu for them to pick from
